title: Angkor
hook: Jayavarman VII, a Buddhist king of Cambodia, and the smiling faces of the Bayon

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sukhothai, and the Buddha cast mid-stride. Your line: the walking Buddha.

Climb the steep stone steps of the Bayon, at the heart of the old city of Angkor Thom in Cambodia, and the faces find you before you find them. A great stone face on a tower, eyes half closed, lips turned up at the corners. Turn your head, and there's another, looking off in a different direction. Then another, on the next tower over. Moss in the cracks, lichen on the cheeks, and still that same calm, closed-mouth smile. Visitors have argued for a long time about whose face it is.
screen: `THE STEPS OF THE BAYON.` → `A FACE ON EVERY TOWER.` → `WHOSE FACE IS IT?`

segments.voice: First, the king. Angkor was the seat of a great Khmer kingdom, and kings there had built huge temples, some of them for Hindu gods, like Vishnu at Angkor Wat. King Jayavarman the Seventh was a Buddhist, of the Mahayana stream, and when he built his walled city he put the Bayon at its center. Second, the question nobody can settle. The temple left no label on the faces. Some scholars see the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, called Lokeshvara in Cambodia. Some see the king himself. Some see both at once: a ruler who wanted to be seen as compassion turned in every direction. The honest answer: nobody knows, and the stone doesn't say. Third, the bodhisattva behind the guess. In the Lotus Sutra, Avalokiteshvara is the one who hears beings who call out in trouble and comes to help, taking whatever form will reach them. A face turned to every point of the compass fits that picture well. Fourth, what the king's own words add. Inscriptions from his reign tell of hospitals and rest houses he founded, and one hospital inscription says, in substance, that the suffering of his people was his own pain. A king can say beautiful things, and historians weigh them carefully. But it is the same idea as the towers: a face that doesn't look away. And the smile itself? It isn't laughing at anything, or grinning for a camera. It has nowhere in particular to point: gentle, a little inward, offered to whoever happens to be standing there.
screen: `JAYAVARMAN VII, A BUDDHIST KING AT ANGKOR.` · `WHOSE FACES? NOBODY CAN SAY FOR SURE.` · `LOKESHVARA HEARS THOSE WHO CALL.` · `THEIR SUFFERING WAS HIS PAIN.` · then, large: `THE SMILING TOWERS.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes half close like the faces on the towers, and let the corners of your mouth lift just slightly, not a grin, not for anyone. Breathe in and out with the small smile, noticing the eyes, the jaw, the shoulders, and if it fades or feels strange, let it return without fuss.
Angkor. The old Khmer capital in Cambodia, where King Jayavarman the Seventh raised the Bayon and its towers of quiet, smiling faces. Today's word.
Your line: the smiling towers. Whose face it is, the stone still keeps to itself. Day eight hundred eighty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Cambodian Buddhists and visitors from many places come to the Bayon at Angkor Thom, and in Mahayana Buddhism Avalokiteshvara is honored as the bodhisattva of compassion, often called on in chant and prayer.

notes: All paraphrased; nothing quoted. The king is named in voice simply as 'Jayavarman' (he is Jayavarman VII); the regnal number is left out of the voice under the claims rule.

Identification of the Bayon faces (Lokeshvara, the king, or both) presented as open; confirm fairness.
Hospital inscription paraphrase ('the suffering of his people was his own pain'): from the Say Fong / hospital edicts as commonly summarized; confirm.
Lotus Sutra chapter on Avalokiteshvara paraphrased (hears those who call, takes forms to reach them). Kern 1884 is a public-domain English translation if a quote is wanted later.

Audit: the voice said only 'King Jayavarman was a Buddhist'; several Khmer kings bore that name (Jayavarman II is linked with the Hindu devaraja cult), so the bare name was wrong. Restored 'the Seventh' (a regnal name, not a count) in teach, word, screen head and match.
